questions.question: What are the two networks in a GAN, and what do they do?

options.text: Encoder and decoder, which compress and reconstruct
Generator produces samples; discriminator tries to distinguish real from fake
Teacher and student, for knowledge distillation
Actor and critic, for reinforcement learning

questions.explanation: A GAN trains a generator and a discriminator in an adversarial minimax game.

questions.question: What is mode collapse in GAN training?

options.text: The discriminator becoming too weak to train further
The generator producing only a limited variety of outputs, ignoring large parts of the data distribution
Gradients exploding in the generator
The loss function going negative

questions.explanation: Mode collapse occurs when the generator maps many latent vectors to few outputs, failing to cover the true data distribution.

questions.question: Wasserstein GAN replaces Jensen-Shannon divergence with which metric?

options.text: KL divergence
Earth Mover's (Wasserstein-1) distance
L2 distance in pixel space
Hellinger distance

questions.explanation: WGAN minimizes the Earth Mover's distance, which provides smoother gradients even when distributions don't overlap.

questions.question: Spectral normalization constrains each layer's:

options.text: Mean activation to be zero
Largest singular value (spectral norm), enforcing 1-Lipschitz continuity
L1 norm of weights
Number of parameters

questions.explanation: Dividing weights by their largest singular value keeps the discriminator 1-Lipschitz, stabilizing training in WGAN and related formulations.

questions.question: What innovation does StyleGAN introduce in its generator architecture?

options.text: A purely convolutional encoder
A mapping network plus adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) injecting styles at each resolution
Reinforcement learning for generation
A transformer-only architecture

questions.explanation: StyleGAN maps latent z to intermediate w, then injects w via AdaIN at each scale — disentangling coarse and fine style attributes.

questions.question: In the original GAN paper, what practical modification is recommended for the generator's loss to avoid vanishing gradients early in training?

options.text: Minimize log(1 − D(G(z))) as stated in the minimax objective
Maximize log D(G(z)) instead, providing stronger gradients when D easily rejects fakes
Use L2 pixel loss between generated and real images
Train the generator twice for every discriminator step

questions.explanation: When the generator is poor, D(G(z)) ≈ 0 and the gradient of log(1 − D(G(z))) is nearly flat. Maximizing log D(G(z)) instead gives a much stronger gradient signal early in training. This is the 'non-saturating' loss recommended in Goodfellow et al. (2014).

questions.question: A GAN achieves a low FID score but a low Inception Score. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The GAN has collapsed to a single mode
The generated images are realistic and diverse but do not clearly belong to recognizable ImageNet classes
The FID calculation has a bug
The GAN is overfitting to the training set

questions.explanation: IS relies on the Inception classifier producing confident per-class predictions and diverse marginal class coverage. If a GAN generates realistic images that don’t map neatly onto ImageNet categories (e.g., abstract textures, medical images), IS will be low even though FID — which compares feature distributions directly — correctly reflects the quality. This is why FID is the preferred primary metric.

questions.question: In WGAN-GP, the gradient penalty is computed on interpolated samples x̂ = εx_real + (1−ε)x_fake. Why are interpolated samples used instead of just real or fake samples?

options.text: To reduce computational cost by halving the batch size needed
Because the 1-Lipschitz constraint must hold everywhere, and interpolations sample the region between the real and generated manifolds where the critic’s gradient matters most
Because the gradient is always zero on real and fake samples
To implement a form of data augmentation that improves discriminator generalization

questions.explanation: The Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality requires the critic to be 1-Lipschitz everywhere, but enforcing this globally is intractable. Gulrajani et al. (2017) showed that for optimal critics the gradient norm is 1 almost everywhere along straight lines between pairs of points from p_data and p_g. Interpolations sample exactly this region — the 'transport path' between distributions — where violations of the Lipschitz constraint would most affect the Wasserstein estimate.

questions.question: In a projection discriminator for conditional GANs (Miyato & Koyama, 2018), how is the class label y incorporated into the discriminator's decision?

options.text: The class label is concatenated with the image as an additional input channel
The discriminator's feature vector is projected (inner product) with a learned class embedding, adding a class-specific bias to the realness score
A separate classification head predicts the class, and its loss is added to the adversarial loss
Class-conditional batch normalization replaces all normalization layers in the discriminator

questions.explanation: The projection discriminator computes an inner product between the discriminator's feature representation φ(x) and a learned class embedding ψ(y), effectively adding a class-specific term to the discriminator score. This is more stable than naive concatenation (option A, which dilutes the conditioning signal) and avoids the training interference of auxiliary classifiers (option C, which is AC-GAN). Class-conditional batch norm (option D) is used in the generator (e.g., BigGAN), not the discriminator.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of diffusion models over GANs?

options.text: Diffusion models generate images in a single forward pass, making them faster
Diffusion models use stable training (no adversarial game) and achieve better mode coverage, but require many iterative denoising steps at inference
Diffusion models require no neural networks, only statistical sampling
Diffusion models always produce higher resolution images than GANs

questions.explanation: Diffusion models train a denoiser with a simple MSE loss (no adversarial instability) and naturally cover the full data distribution (no mode collapse). The trade-off is inference speed: generating a single image requires hundreds of sequential denoising steps (though techniques like DDIM and consistency models reduce this). GANs remain faster at inference (single forward pass) but harder to train stably.

questions.question: In Progressive Growing of GANs (PGGAN), what is the purpose of the fade-in mechanism when adding new higher-resolution layers?

options.text: It pre-trains the new layers independently before connecting them to the rest of the network
It linearly interpolates between the upsampled lower-resolution output and the new higher-resolution layers using a blending factor α that increases from 0 to 1 during training
It freezes the existing layers and only trains the new ones until they converge
It doubles the learning rate for the new layers to help them catch up with the trained layers

questions.explanation: The fade-in mechanism smoothly transitions from one resolution to the next by blending: G_new = (1-α)·upsample(G_old) + α·G_additional, where α linearly increases from 0 to 1. This prevents the sudden introduction of untrained layers from destabilizing the already-learned lower-resolution representations. Option A is wrong because the layers are not pretrained in isolation. Option C is wrong because all layers continue training during fade-in. Option D is wrong because no learning rate doubling is used.

questions.question: Which architectural guideline from the DCGAN paper (Radford et al., 2016) replaces deterministic spatial pooling layers in the discriminator?

options.text: Max pooling with larger kernel sizes
Strided convolutions, allowing the network to learn its own spatial downsampling
Average pooling followed by a fully connected layer
Dilated convolutions to increase receptive field without reducing resolution

questions.explanation: DCGAN replaced all pooling layers with strided convolutions (discriminator) and fractional-strided convolutions (generator). This lets the network learn its own downsampling/upsampling functions rather than using fixed pooling operations. Combined with batch normalization, ReLU in the generator, and LeakyReLU in the discriminator, these guidelines became the standard recipe for convolutional GANs. Max pooling (option A) loses spatial information deterministically. Average pooling + FC (option C) was the pre-DCGAN approach. Dilated convolutions (option D) don't downsample at all.

questions.question: In BigGAN, the 'truncation trick' resamples latent vectors z from a truncated normal distribution N(0, I; |z_i| < ψ). What is the effect of decreasing the truncation threshold ψ from 2.0 to 0.5?

options.text: Generated images become more diverse but lower quality, as the model explores unusual regions of latent space
Generated images become higher quality but less diverse, as latent vectors concentrate near the distribution's mean
Training becomes more stable because extreme gradient values are avoided
The discriminator becomes easier to fool because truncated inputs are always classified as real

questions.explanation: The truncation trick trades diversity for quality at inference time (it does not affect training — option C is wrong). A smaller ψ constrains z closer to the origin where the generator has seen the most training signal, producing higher-fidelity but less varied samples. A larger ψ allows exploration of the latent space periphery, increasing diversity but risking artifacts. This is a post-hoc inference-time control — the BigGAN paper showed that IS improves monotonically as ψ decreases, while FID has a sweet spot (too low ψ hurts FID due to lost diversity). Option D is wrong because the truncation trick operates at inference, not during adversarial training.

questions.question: CycleGAN enables unpaired image-to-image translation (e.g., horse → zebra) without aligned training pairs. What is the key architectural mechanism that makes this possible?

options.text: A single generator with a domain label fed as an extra input channel
Two generator-discriminator pairs with a cycle-consistency loss that enforces F(G(x)) ≈ x and G(F(y)) ≈ y
A shared encoder with two separate decoders, one per domain
A pre-trained classifier that provides domain labels as supervision

questions.explanation: CycleGAN (Zhu et al., 2017) uses two generators (G: X→Y, F: Y→X) and two discriminators (D_X, D_Y). The cycle-consistency loss enforces round-trip reconstruction: translating from domain X to Y and back should recover the original image. This constraint replaces the need for paired training data (as in Pix2Pix) by ensuring the mappings preserve content while changing style. Option A describes StarGAN's approach to multi-domain translation. Option C describes a shared-encoder architecture (like UNIT). Option D would require labeled pairs, defeating the purpose of unpaired translation.
